transcript.content: Hello, I am Dr. Smith. Could you please tell me what brings you in to see me today?

I'm here because I've been struggling with really extreme and exhausting mood swings for over a year now. I alternate between periods where I have intense energy and get very irritable, and other times when I fall into a deep depression with no motivation at all. It's just been a constant, exhausting cycle that I can't seem to control.

During those periods of intense energy, have you ever had symptoms so severe that you required hospitalization, or did you experience a complete break from reality, such as hearing or seeing things that weren't there?

No, I've never been hospitalized during those high-energy periods, even though they get pretty intense. I also haven't ever experienced any hallucinations, like hearing or seeing things that aren't actually there.

During those high-energy periods, do you feel like you are still able to function at work or home, or are the symptoms severe enough that they clearly interfere with your ability to carry out your daily responsibilities?

Yes, they definitely interfere with my life and cause serious problems at home and work. I end up starting way too many projects at once, and I've made some really reckless business investments and spent excessive amounts of money we can't afford. It has created a lot of financial distress and chaos for my family.
How long do these high-energy periods typically last before your mood shifts back to depression?
The high-energy periods usually last for about a year and a month before my mood shifts. Once I fall into the depressive phase, that typically lasts for about 11 months.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient reports prolonged periods of high energy and irritability lasting over a year, which meet criteria for mania rather than hypomania given the severe impairment in functioning, financial distress, and reckless behavior. The presence of major depressive episodes alternating with these manic episodes supports a diagnosis of Bipolar I Disorder.
